---
title: "Before the first call"
subtitle: "Ten minutes of setup, done once"
---

Nothing to install. You need a device that can join the call, a second window (or a second device) for your AI assistant, a web browser, and **one account**: an AI assistant. Nothing else in this course depends on a particular tool, a verification step, or anyone's approval.

## 1. One account

| Tool | Why you need it | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **A general assistant**: ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini (any one; a free account is enough), or another you already use | Drafting and structuring in every lab | Sign up with your own email and sign in on the device you will use for the labs |

Use your own account on your own device. Do not use a shared login. No account yet, or it will not open? Say so in the chat: follow a shared screen and you can still do every exercise.

## 2. The second option, for the tool comparisons

[Lab 1](day1/lab1-templates-and-limits.qmd) and [Lab 2](day2/lab2-one-case-three-outputs.qmd) compare your assistant with something that shows its sources. You do **not** need a special account for that. [Module 3](day1/m3-choosing-tools.qmd#second-option) gives three ways to do it, and on the day you use the first one you can open:

1. A literature-grounded tool, if you can open one.
2. Your assistant's own search or citation mode, if it has one.
3. A plain literature search, such as PubMed or your library's database. No AI and no account.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## If you want to try a literature-grounded tool
Vera Health is one example. It is for healthcare professionals, in practice or in training, and its home page says to sign up with your professional credentials, so try it a few days early. What it asks, and what it says about who can use it, is in [Module 3](day1/m3-choosing-tools.qmd#different-doctor). Treat it as a bonus: if it does not work for you, nothing in the course breaks.
:::

## 3. Practice data is synthetic

Every lab uses the [case cards](reference/case-cards.qmd): five fictional patients. **Do not type a real patient's name, ID, or details into any tool during this course.** The reason is the whole of Day Three, but the rule starts now. If you want to use a case of your own, read the [privacy checklist](reference/privacy-checklist.qmd) first, and if you are not certain it is safe, use a card.

## 4. Your screen on the call

- **Best:** one laptop with two windows side by side, the call and the slides in one and your assistant in the other.
- **Also good:** the call on one screen or device and your assistant on another.
- **A phone alone** is a squeeze for a lab. If it is all you have, say so in the chat and your instructor will adjust.
- **The slides.** Your instructor shares them, and the link goes in the chat. Open it in a window of your own: you can go at your own pace, and copy a prompt straight from a slide.
- **Join a few minutes early** to check that you can hear, be heard, and type in the chat. Mute when you are not speaking.

## 5. How you take part

Every activity is one of five moves, and the slide says which, with a time.

| Move | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Chat** | Everyone types at once; the instructor reads a few out |
| **Speak** | Two or three of you unmute when asked |
| **Share** | One person shares a screen when asked |
| **Pair** | A breakout room of two, a few minutes |
| **Solo** | Your own device, your own assistant |

## 6. What to have ready each day

| Day | Have ready |
|---|---|
| **One** | Your device, your assistant signed in, and a place to save prompts (a notes app is fine, with no patient information in it) |
| **Two** | Your favorite prompt from Day One, and an idea of a *type* of case you present or teach (no patient information) |
| **Three** | Your saved output from Lab 1, "break it on purpose", with its warning line, and one AI output from Days One and Two to put through the three-question check |

## 7. Check your setup

Two minutes. Tick each one.

- [ ] I can join the call, hear, and type in the chat.
- [ ] I can open my general assistant, sign in, and send it a message, with the call open beside it.
- [ ] I know which second option I will try first for the comparisons in Labs 1 and 2. Any of the three is fine.
- [ ] I can copy text from a web page and paste it into a chat.
- [ ] I have somewhere to save text, and I know where it is.
- [ ] I can open the slides link in a window of its own.

## 8. Ground rules for the call

- **Candor over polish.** The labs are built to make the tools fail. A tool failing is the point, and saying so in the chat helps everyone.
- **Synthetic only.** No real patient information, in any lab, in any tool.
- **Your device, your account.** Do not sign in with an institutional account you would not want to explain.
- **Ask.** Type it in the chat or unmute. The best questions usually start with "but what if".

If something goes wrong, the [troubleshooting page](reference/troubleshooting.qmd) covers the common cases.
